Scope warning. This paper demonstrates an end-to-end provenance architecture and reports feasibility, usability, descriptive agreement, knowledge-graph construction, and operating-cost observations. It does not establish diagnostic accuracy of INSPECT-AI, validity of all 21 INSPECT-SR checks, or superiority to manual research-integrity assessment.

External repositories, model guides, live knowledge graphs, APIs, and web interfaces referenced by the paper were not independently verified in this SEA run. Appraisal is based on the evaluated PDF.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis. The paper argues that LLM-assisted research-integrity assessment should be treated as a human-supervised decision process whose evidence, automated suggestions, reviewer overrides, rationales, and provenance can be represented semantically and published as a reusable knowledge graph.
What the source reports
  • INSPECT-AI semi-automates four INSPECT-SR checks using PDF extraction, external evidence retrieval, predefined conditional rules, and human confirmation/override.
  • RIPE-O models the provenance of assessments using TIDO/PROV-O plus bibliographic ontologies.
  • RIPE-KG contains 140 assessments of 95 publications and supports queryable provenance, reviewer comparisons, author-network exploration, and federation with scholarly graphs.
  • Automated and human outcomes agreed on 444 of 514 question-level pairs (86.4%), but disagreement was strongly concentrated in study-registration judgments.
Independent appraisal
  • The strongest contribution is the provenance/data architecture, not the LLM itself.
  • The disagreement data are evidence for preserving decision provenance and human rationale; they are not an accuracy benchmark because no adjudicated gold standard is reported and human reviewers themselves disagree.
  • Implementation transparency is unusually strong for a prototype paper, but empirical validation is still early and the tool covers only 4 of the 21 INSPECT-SR checks.
  • The system is most useful as a design reference for auditable human-in-the-loop evidence assessment, not as evidence that automated integrity screening can safely replace expert review.

Section-by-section condensation

Abstract

The authors introduce three linked artifacts: INSPECT-AI for LLM-assisted, human-reviewed RCT integrity assessment; RIPE-O for semantic provenance representation; and RIPE-KG for publishing assessment traces. The abstract positions the work as a response to the manual burden and subjectivity of research-integrity assessment and reports an initial graph of 140 expert assessments covering 95 RCT publications.

1. Introduction

The paper motivates integrity assessment by emphasizing that problematic RCTs can propagate into systematic reviews and clinical guidance. Manual integrity checks are described as labor-intensive because reviewers must inspect retractions, comments, author histories, registration data, and publication content across multiple sources. INSPECT-AI is framed as efficiency support rather than autonomous adjudication.

The second argument is that disagreement is intrinsic to this work. The authors therefore extend FAIR-style thinking from research outputs to the provenance of assessment decisions, motivating an observatory that stores evidence, agent actions, reviewer judgments, and rationales in a knowledge graph.

2. Related Work

The source situates RIPE-KG among scholarly graphs such as OpenAIRE, Scholia, Semantic Scholar, ORKG, and SemOpenAlex, arguing that these resources generally do not represent publication trustworthiness assessments. It also contrasts INSPECT-AI with integrity checklists such as TRACT, RIA, CPC-TST, and REAPPRAISED and notes prior semi-automation experiments.

INSPECT-SR is the governing assessment framework for the prototype. It contains 21 checks across post-publication notices, conduct/governance/transparency, text/figure inspection, and result/statistical checks; this paper automates only a subset.

3. Methodology

Development was interdisciplinary and iterative. The team used agile prototyping, 50 diverse examples of problematic publications, and repeated engagement with biomedical researchers and evidence-synthesis groups. The source explicitly reports that this process pushed the design toward human-in-the-loop operation rather than full automation.

RIPE-O was developed with the four-stage Linked Open Terms methodology. Competency questions were derived from selected INSPECT-SR checks and the 7W provenance framing. The ontology extends TIDO/PROV-O, reuses FABIO/CITO and other bibliographic vocabularies, and was implemented with Protégé/WIDOCO. INSPECT-AI JSON process logs are transformed to RDF through YARRRML mappings.

4. INSPECT-AI Tool

After PDF upload, GROBID extracts standard bibliographic metadata while Gemini 2.0 Flash extracts trial identifiers and timeline information. LLM-derived evidence includes an explanation intended to speed reviewer verification. DOI/title and registration identifiers trigger queries to external resources including Retraction Watch, PubPeer, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP.

Evidence is evaluated against predefined rules to generate suggested Yes/No/Unclear outcomes. Reviewers inspect evidence and can accept, modify, or override suggestions and record a rationale. Evidence, assessments, and participating agents are logged in PostgreSQL, making later provenance reconstruction possible.

4.1 Pilot Deployment

Thirteen volunteers across Aberdeen, Manchester, and Indiana University tested the system in October-November 2025. They independently assessed 69 publications and generated 104 assessment traces. The publication set included papers with known trustworthiness issues, while reviewers could also select their own papers.

Most participants had systematic-review experience (77%); 61.5% had previously performed RCT integrity assessments. Forty-six percent rated the tool easy/very easy, 69% fairly/very user-friendly, and 69% quick/very quick. No participant selected difficult-to-use or not-user-friendly responses. These observations support basic feasibility/acceptance but do not quantify time savings, accuracy, or comparative performance.

5. RIPE-O

RIPE-O is designed to capture provenance for mixed automated and human assessment processes without prescribing specific integrity questions. Its core model represents assessed works, assessments, questions, hypotheses, evidence, evidence-aggregation and evaluation activities, and human/software agents, all linked through PROV/TIDO-style generation, use, attribution, and association relations.

Evidence subclasses include retraction/correction notices, expressions of concern, peer comments, registry evidence, study-design evidence, and publication details. The ontology was checked with OOPS! and its competency questions were operationalized as SPARQL queries against real assessment data transformed into RIPE-KG.

6. RIPE-KG

At the time of writing, RIPE-KG contains 140 assessments of 95 distinct publications, 927 distinct author entities across assessed publications/references/PubPeer comments, and 1,221 integrity hypotheses. Reviewer identities are pseudonymized while retaining reviewer-role distinctions. JSON logs are transformed into RDF with YARRRML mappings.

Author disambiguation combines GROBID extraction with OpenAlex identifiers and SemOpenAlex links. For assessed-publication authors, 1,202 author mentions were consolidated into 875 local RIPE author instances; 766 were linked to SemOpenAlex and 109 (12.5%) remained unlinked because metadata were absent or mismatched.

6.1 Analysing Assessment Outputs

The current system implements four checks: main-publication retraction, expression-of-concern/other post-publication notice, concerns arising from other publications by the research team, and timing/absence of trial registration. Among 514 question-level automated/human pairs, 444 agreed (86.4%) and 70 disagreed (13.6%). Disagreement was 8.5% for retraction status, 3.9% for post-publication notices, 15.6% for research-team concerns, and 26.2% for study registration.

Repeated human reviews also varied. Across 22 multiply assessed publications, question-level agreement was 83.3% for retractions, 84.2% for post-publication notices, 94.4% for research-team concerns, but only 44.4% for registration. For overall integrity judgments, 16 of 22 repeatedly reviewed works (72.7%) received the same category and 6 (27.3%) did not. One work received eight assessments spanning all three overall categories. The source interprets this variability as a reason to retain provenance and rationale rather than collapse assessments to opaque labels.

6.2 Author Networks

A SPARQL example shows how RIPE-KG can identify author pairs who repeatedly coauthor works that received at least one human “serious-concerns” assessment. This demonstrates a graph-analytic use case beyond single-publication review, although the paper does not validate such network signals as predictors of misconduct or unreliability.

6.3 External Scholarly-KG Integration

RIPE works can be federated with SemOpenAlex through owl:sameAs links. The paper demonstrates a query that retrieves human-reviewed overall integrity outcomes for works assigned to an external field classification (Endocrinology), illustrating how provenance-rich integrity data can be combined with broader scholarly metadata.

6.4 Costs

The source reports approximately US$79.53 in operational cost during the October-November 2025 pilot. A single VPS (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM) cost $77 and Gemini 2.0 Flash extraction cost $1.34; the reported marginal LLM cost per paper was below $0.10.

Appraisal note: the two explicitly itemized components sum to $78.34, leaving $1.19 of the stated total unitemized in the paper. Human reviewer labor and development labor are not presented as part of this operating-cost calculation.

7. Limitations

The authors identify incomplete INSPECT-SR coverage, dependence on OpenAlex for disambiguation, and sensitivity to the completeness/quality of SemOpenAlex, Retraction Watch, and PubPeer. Elsewhere in the paper they also describe practical limits in retrieving publisher-site retraction information behind firewall protections.

8. Conclusions

The authors position the work as an end-to-end FAIR provenance pipeline for integrity assessment and as reusable infrastructure for integrating outputs from multiple current or future integrity tools. They argue that observed human-human and human-automation disagreements make human validation and provenance preservation central requirements for accountable LLM-assisted assessment.

9. Future Work

Planned work includes expanding INSPECT-SR coverage, applying RIPE-O beyond the present biomedical context, expanding community/expert assessments, restricting contribution pathways to trusted users, and using graph-based selection mechanisms to identify publications for future human review.

10–11. Acknowledgments & Generative-AI declaration

The project reports ESRC grant support and additional institutional support. The authors disclose GenAI use for LaTeX formatting, text-shortening suggestions, and programming assistance including query/code generation for INSPECT-AI and the RIPE-KG interface.

Supported inference: automated suggestions and final human judgments are not interchangeable, and disagreement is task-dependent. The data strongly justify retaining question-level evidence and reviewer rationale.
Not established: 86.4% raw agreement is not equivalent to 86.4% accuracy. The paper does not report an adjudicated reference standard, chance-corrected agreement, confidence intervals, sensitivity/specificity, calibration, or prospective error rates.

Study registration is the conspicuous weak point for inter-reviewer consistency. The paper attributes this to the domain judgment required to decide whether registration, recruitment, and study timelines are compatible with acceptable trial practice. Evaluation & appraisal

Verdict: Read first. High-value design reference for transparent, provenance-first LLM-assisted scientific assessment. Treat the empirical pilot as feasibility evidence, not as validation that INSPECT-AI is accurate enough for autonomous or practice-level use.

Relevance 9/10

Rationale: Directly addresses auditable LLM-assisted literature assessment, provenance, human override, and reusable structured evidence.

Evidence basis: End-to-end tool + ontology + KG + query examples.

Limiting factor: Focus is research integrity of RCT publications rather than general evidence extraction/appraisal.

Would rise/fall: Broader demonstrated use across evidence-assessment tasks would raise it; a narrower tool-only contribution would lower it.

Novelty 8/10

Rationale: The integration of human-reviewed integrity assessment with explicit semantic decision provenance and an open KG is distinctive.

Evidence basis: RIPE-O/RIPE-KG architecture, mappings, persistent identifiers, queryable human/automated hypotheses.

Limiting factor: Independent priority/novelty claims were not externally verified.

Would rise/fall: Demonstrated interoperability with multiple independent assessment tools would strengthen the novelty claim.

Method strength 6/10

Rationale: Engineering and ontology methods are explicit, but the human-subject pilot is small and descriptive.

Evidence basis: LOT methodology, competency questions, OOPS!/SPARQL validation, 13-person pilot, real publication assessments.

Limiting factor: No controlled comparator, gold standard, prespecified statistical evaluation, or rigorous reliability analysis.

Would rise/fall: Prospective blinded validation against adjudicated expert consensus and objective workflow-time measures would raise this substantially.

Evidence strength 5/10

Rationale: Data support feasibility and the existence of meaningful disagreement, but not screening accuracy or effectiveness.

Evidence basis: 514 paired outcomes, repeated human assessments, pilot usability, graph counts.

Limiting factor: Raw agreement lacks a truth standard and uncertainty estimates; sample selection was partly enriched with known problematic publications.

Would rise/fall: External validation, error adjudication, class-balanced performance metrics, and measured reviewer-efficiency gains would raise the score.

External validity 4/10

Rationale: The evaluated deployment is narrow in institutions, reviewers, publication selection, domain, and check coverage.

Evidence basis: 13 volunteers, 69 pilot publications, four implemented INSPECT-SR checks, 95 works in the graph.

Limiting factor: The publication sample is not presented as representative of routine systematic-review screening.

Would rise/fall: Multi-center deployments with consecutive or randomly sampled RCTs and additional disciplines/checks would raise it.

Implementation value 9/10

Rationale: The paper exposes a concrete architecture with provenance types, mappings, IDs, query patterns, human-override semantics, and operating-cost detail.

Evidence basis: Workflow, ontology, SPARQL listings, KG construction, author disambiguation, UI figures, permanent resource identifiers.

Limiting factor: Some implementation detail is delegated to external repositories/guides not evaluated here.

Would rise/fall: A formal end-to-end reproducibility package and independent replication would raise it further.

Main strengths

  • Separates evidence, automated hypotheses, human hypotheses, activities, and agents rather than storing only a final label.
  • Design explicitly treats LLM outputs as suggestions with reviewer correction/override.
  • Uses established semantic-web/provenance standards and permanent identifiers.
  • Shows practical query use cases rather than presenting the ontology only as a conceptual artifact.
  • Reports disagreement rather than hiding it; the data expose where human judgment is hardest.
  • Documents cost and author-disambiguation coverage with concrete counts.

Main limitations / risks

  • Only four of 21 INSPECT-SR checks are implemented.
  • No gold-standard accuracy benchmark for the LLM/rule pipeline or final assessments.
  • Human reviewers are not a stable reference standard; registration agreement is particularly low.
  • Known-problematic publications were deliberately included in the pilot, limiting prevalence/generalization interpretations.
  • External-source incompleteness and publisher-access barriers can cause missing or misleading evidence.
  • OpenAlex-dependent identity resolution leaves 12.5% of assessed-publication author instances unlinked.
  • Author-network analysis can be useful for prioritization but could invite guilt-by-association if interpreted as evidence of individual misconduct; the paper does not validate such signals for that purpose.
  • The reported pilot cost is not a full economic evaluation and does not report reviewer/development labor.

Confidence in appraisal

High for source interpretation; moderate for broader performance implications. The architecture, workflow, counts, and descriptive analyses are clearly reported. Claims about accuracy, generalizability, or comparative efficiency remain limited because the paper does not provide the study design needed to establish them.

Implementation / research takeaways

Preserve dual hypothesesStore automated suggestion and human final judgment as separate attributed objects. An override should not erase the model output.
Provenance is a first-class outputRecord evidence origin, extraction rationale, activity, agent, timestamps/versions, question, outcome, and reviewer rationale—not just a final concern category.
Validate by task, not aggregate agreementRegistration assessment behaves differently from simple retraction/notice lookup. Performance and review requirements should be check-specific.
Keep deterministic rules visibleThe prototype uses predefined conditional logic after evidence aggregation. That separation makes failures easier to audit than an end-to-end opaque model judgment.
Model identity uncertaintyAuthor disambiguation is a substantive safety boundary. Name collisions can directly create false concern signals, as shown in Table 2.
Use KGs for audit before predictionThe strongest demonstrated KG uses are trace inspection, disagreement analysis, and federation. Predictive “untrustworthy publication” discovery is future work, not a validated result.
Do not overclaim from this paper: it does not show that LLMs can reliably determine RCT trustworthiness, that 86.4% agreement is clinically acceptable accuracy, that the RIPE-KG is representative of the literature, or that author-network concern counts should be used as misconduct scores.
